I wanted the sound to believe her for a few seconds.

turns.speaker: Dev Malik
turns.text: A documentary interview can be pushed around very easily by music. The person may sound evasive simply because the arrangement has told you to distrust a pause. Where music does enter, it belongs to the film's movement between versions of the interview, rather than pretending to reveal what the speaker secretly means.

records.title: Cressida Maraschino: Back on Set
records.details: June asks Cressida about returning for a guest role after decades away from regular production. A short oral-history exchange recorded during a quiet break.

turns.speaker: June Park
turns.text: Did you want to watch the old films before coming back?

turns.speaker: Cressida Maraschino
turns.text: No. You can end up trying to impersonate yourself. I wanted to know where the chair was, who had been in the room before me and why nobody wanted to mention the missing take. Those are useful questions. Whether I could still raise an eyebrow exactly as I did in nineteen sixty-four was not a useful question.

turns.speaker: June Park
turns.text: You asked to walk the entrance without the camera.

turns.speaker: Cressida Maraschino
turns.text: At my age, knowing where the floor changes matters. Then I could stop thinking about the floor and listen to the person in front of me.

turns.speaker: June Park
turns.text: Did the guest part feel like a farewell?

turns.speaker: Cressida Maraschino
turns.text: A working day. A good one. If somebody wants a farewell, they can write one in the programme. I had a scene to do.

records.title: Lucia Ferrer: After the Rain
records.details: A field interview about the previous night’s location wrap, rehearsing physical action and doing her own stunt work. Recorded for Lucia’s working archive rather than a studio press kit.

turns.speaker: Lucia Ferrer
turns.text: The photograph from last night looks dramatic because of the rain. By then we were mostly thinking about wet coats and the last equipment cases. The interesting preparation had happened much earlier. We walked the route before the camera arrived, then rehearsed the scene until the movement and the dialogue belonged to the same thought. I perform all my own stunts. I have never used a stunt double. That does not make it a solo job. The coordinator, the camera crew and the other performers all know things I need to know. I want the preparation to be shared so that, during the take, I can concentrate on the person in front of me. In this scene the escort is always moving and the handler is almost still. If I add movement simply to make my part look harder, I take something away from his part. The work is knowing when the action has already said enough.

records.title: The Doorway and the Pause
records.details: Lucia and Darius compare the moving escort and the watchful handler in their courier-film collaboration. An informal two-person debrief about where action gives way to hesitation.

turns.speaker: Darius King
turns.text: I thought the handler should give away very little. Then I saw Lucia rehearse the entrance and realised that doing nothing could become a very large gesture beside that movement.

turns.speaker: Lucia Ferrer
turns.text: The escort knows where she is going. That is useful until she reaches somebody who refuses to move. We tried making the pause shorter, but it let her win the scene too easily.

turns.speaker: Darius King
turns.text: In the version we kept, I look at the case before I look at her. It is a small delay. It gives him a history without asking him to explain it.

turns.speaker: Lucia Ferrer
turns.text: And it gives me something to answer. Not another piece of action, just the decision to stay in the doorway for a moment longer.

turns.speaker: Darius King
turns.text: The preparation was quite precise. The pleasure is that the finished exchange does not look like two people congratulating themselves on their timing.

render.input_policy: Each authored speaker turn is split only at sentence boundaries before synthesis with its recorded stock voice and speed. The longest resulting chunk is 168 characters, conservatively below Kokoro's 510 phoneme-token truncation limit.
render.assembly: Sentence chunks are joined with deterministic 0.14 to 0.22 second pauses into one ignored raw WAV per authored turn. Turn WAVs are joined in authored order with deterministic 0.30 to 0.68 second conversational pauses.
